*   **Output:** A set of triangles (or meta-cells) marked as visible, forwarded to the graphics accelerator for final rasterization [S2, book].

It differs from view-independent methods by performing coarse software visibility tests during octree traversal to prune hidden cells before forwarding triangulations to the graphics accelerator [S2, book].

The claim states that the method differs from view-independent methods by performing coarse software visibility tests during octree traversal to prune hidden cells before forwarding triangulations to the graphics accelerator. The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly describes a three-step approach: 1) traversing the octree front-to-back and pruning empty subtrees; 2) performing 'coarse software visibility tests' on cells to determine if they are hidden by previously extracted sections (pruning); and 3) forwarding the triangulation of visible cells to the graphics accelerator. It also contrasts this with view-independent methods which extract both visible and hidden portions. Thus, every fact in the claim is supported by the text.

It describes the algorithm's steps, including front-to-back traversal, pruning based on min-max values, coarse software visibility tests, and forwarding visible cells to graphics hardware (Section 47.3, Figure 47.5 description). It also mentions hierarchical tiles and shear-warp factorization for acceleration (Section 47.3.2, 47.3.2.1).

Visibility tests add cost but prune hidden cells, reducing total work [S2, book].

The evidence explicitly states that visibility tests are performed to determine if cells are hidden, allowing them to be pruned. It notes that 'A hidden cell, and all of its children, will not be traversed further and thus can justify the time and effort invested in the classification,' implying that while the test adds cost, it reduces total work by avoiding traversal and rendering of hidden cells. The text also mentions that 'if one can extract just the visible portions of the isosurface, the number of rendered polygons will be reduced, resulting in a faster algorithm.' Thus, the claim that visibility tests add cost but prune hidden cells, reducing total work, is fully supported.
